lines: A row surviving inside its own file is one thing. A whole column surviving across an entire table, through a rename or a reorder, is a much bigger ask.
That's an old problem resurfacing at a new altitude, and today it finally gets a real fix, built and checked directly.
Picture a schema change that does two things at once: an existing column gets a new name, and a brand new column gets slotted in right before it.
If whatever reads that table afterward still trusts each column's position in the file to tell it what's what, does the data come back correctly, or not?
answer: Not even close. The moment that new column gets inserted anywhere but the very end, position stops meaning anything reliable.
Every column sitting after the insertion point quietly starts holding some other column's real value instead of its own.

lines: And this was checked directly, not just asserted. A real table on disk, renamed and reordered the exact same way, read back by trusting position alone.
Exactly as feared — the newly inserted column silently inherited the next column's actual value, and every column after that slid one slot out of place.
Here's the real fix, straight from the format's own rules. Every column gets a permanent identity assigned to it once, the moment it's created, and that identity never changes again.
A rename is free to change what a column is called. It is never allowed to touch that permanent identity underneath.
Checked again, on that very same file, this time trusting that permanent identity instead of position.
The renamed column resolved correctly, with its real original data intact. And the genuinely new column, exactly as it should, came back reporting nothing there yet.
Now flip to a format whose files carry ordinary column names instead of that permanent identity scheme. How could a rename possibly avoid rewriting such a file?
Does it just always pay the cost of a full rewrite every time, or is there some other trick available?
answer: There's another trick, and it's the more interesting answer. A separate, stable internal name gets tracked in the table's own metadata, apart from whatever name a person actually sees and uses.
A rename only has to update that metadata record. The underlying file itself never has to move or change at all.

lines: But first, the honest baseline, also checked for real. Without that separate stable internal name in place, the file's own column name really is the only name there is.
So renaming a column under that setup genuinely does force a real rewrite of the file — confirmed directly, not assumed.
Now with that separate stable name actually turned on, checked the same way. The documentation promises renaming shouldn't require touching the underlying file at all.
And it held up byte for byte — the file that came out the other side was completely, provably identical to the one that went in.
Here's what makes this worth remembering. That same permanent-identity trick isn't just about surviving a rename.
It's exactly what also lets a table safely grow a brand new column, widen a type without breaking old readers, or let a nested structure evolve underneath everyone's feet.
So here's the whole idea in one line. A permanent identity, not a name and not a position, is what actually lets a column survive change.
Every trick in this topic — surviving a rename, a reorder, a new type, a nested structure — ultimately traces back to that one same guarantee.
